'might'

I don't think people understand how important bees actually are to global ecology.
How important are they avatar? TELL ME!

bees pollinate a significant proportion (I think it's somewhere between 15 and 30% for the US) of our agricultural crop. that figure is an overall figure- that is- it includes agricultural crop used for animal consumption as well as human consumption. not to mention the native, specialised bees which pollinate respective native plant species.

if we lose a large proportion of multiple bee species, we lose a large proportion of our pollination capabilities. while, in the long-term, we'd recover with other methods of pollination, the short term consequences range from food shortages for particular crops (eg. kiwifruit is pollinated by bumblebees, losing bumblebees reduces kiwifruit availability) on the agricultural scale and a decrease in biological diversity on the ecological scale.

native bee species develop symbiotic, codependent relationships with native plants. they alone develop unique, specialised, efficient means of pollinating native plants. introduced (and more common) bee populations such as honeybees and bumblebees lack this specialised pollination method, so their method of pollinating native plants is inefficient. the local plant population's diversity and population can't be sustained by the unfamiliar bees, hence, they're largely dependent on native pollinators (not just bees; birds, bats and weather can also play a vital role) to reproduce.

if the native bee population is ravaged by an unchecked disease, as the bee population dwindles, so too does the plant population and it's diversity, resulting in long-term endangerment and slowed evolution for the plant species.

the agricultural impact is less severe, mainly because we have a number of different bees which can pollinate the same plant (albeit with different levels of efficiency). unless we lose all kinds of bees over time, agriculture would continue (at a slowed rate) without specific bee species pollinating crops. the problem arises from endangerment of bee species which pollinate a large variety of agricultural plants, such as honeybees, bumblebees and solitary bees. losing one or more of these species would impede most crop harvests heavily, as other kinds of bees are unable to (or inefficient at) pollinating particular kinds of plants that the listed bee species are adept at pollinating.

in short, no bees = reduced sexual plant reproduction (bad thing for crops, worse for native species). it could result in reduced crop harvests and/or endangerment/extinction of particular plant varieties.

crop shortages caused by reduced pollination could have economic impacts. no honey production could also have economic impacts. there are other bee-related products which too could have economic impacts. don't ask me what kind of economic impact, because I don't know. i'm not an economist, but they're all probably bad. not the most convincing statement, but hopefully you can understand what I'm getting at.

a loss of plant species would reduce global biodiversity. that's a sad thing in itself, but it also carries greater impacts. say a particular fruit tree goes the way of the dodo once the native bee stops pollinating it. what about that fruit pigeon which eats said fruits? what does it do now? how about the spotted fox which eats the fruit pigeon? whole ecosystems would have to re-adapt, it's entirely possible that some species which have no interaction with bees could be effected by their absence.

a world without bees is a different world. love and respect the bees, please!
